title: Comets and asteroids as leftovers of planet formation
text:
I want to talk today about the leftovers of planet formation, because the difference between a comet and an asteroid is essentially a difference of address. Both are debris that never assembled into a planet, but where each body formed determined what it is made of.

Close to the young Sun it was far too warm for ice to survive, so the objects that accumulated there are rocky and metallic. We call them asteroids, and most of them orbit in a broad belt between Mars and Jupiter, kept perpetually stirred up by Jupiter's gravity, which is why they never merged into a planet of their own.

Further out, beyond what astronomers call the snow line, water and other volatile compounds could freeze. The bodies that formed there are mixtures of ice, dust and rock, and those are comets. A comet spends most of its long orbit far from the Sun, dark and inert. As it approaches, the ice does not melt but sublimates, passing directly from solid to gas, releasing trapped dust and forming the glowing coma and the tail. And note that the tail always points away from the Sun, driven by the solar wind and radiation pressure, rather than trailing behind the comet's motion.
points: Comets and asteroids are both debris left over from planet formation.
What they are made of depends on where they formed relative to the Sun.
Asteroids formed in the warm inner region, are rocky and metallic, and mostly orbit between Mars and Jupiter.
Jupiter's gravity prevented the asteroid belt from forming a planet.
Comets formed beyond the snow line and are mixtures of ice and dust.
Near the Sun the ice sublimates, creating the coma and a tail that always points away from the Sun.
